nodes.label: The split: the kit in the app, the server apart
nodes.rationale: UI complexity lives in the app, where it can crash without consequence; to the server a window is a rectangle with an endpoint on the other side. That boundary is the one BeOS had and it is correct.

nodes.label: The UI kit (lib/ui.lua)
nodes.rationale: A library running inside the app's process: view tree, layout, event routing and the generation of drawing commands. If it has a bug the app dies and nothing else.

nodes.label: The app server and window manager
nodes.rationale: Windows, decoration, stacking, focus, workspaces, compositing and input routing, all in Lua except the blit. It knows nothing about views.

nodes.label: The view tree
nodes.rationale: A view is a rectangle in its parent's coordinates, as BView was. Nested coordinates, automatic clipping, bottom-up hit testing, and invalidation by region - damage tracking falls out of the tree rather than out of a heuristic.

nodes.label: Messages as tables with a type field
nodes.rationale: A BMessage was a typed dictionary with a four-byte what; here it is a Lua table with a type, which is the same concept without the marshalling. An input event, a message to the app server and a filesystem read are the same class of thing.

nodes.label: Follow modes, and no constraint solver
nodes.rationale: A solver is thousands of lines with non-obvious behaviour when overdetermined; follow modes are fifty lines and cover 90%. The document described the list form while ui.lua read the set form, and nothing caught it because no application had ever used follow - the entire layout path was dead code that happened to compile.

nodes.label: No locks: coroutines instead of BLoopers
nodes.rationale: In BeOS every BWindow was a thread and forgetting Lock() was the number one source of app bugs; the whole locking API existed because threads shared memory. Here each window is a coroutine, so the class of bug does not exist, and a busy window still does not freeze the others because each yields at its receive.

nodes.label: Draw produces a list of commands
nodes.rationale: gc accumulates tables and sends them in one message. Commands being data allows caching a view's list, logging and replaying drawing, inspecting from the REPL, and redirecting to another display without the app knowing.

nodes.label: The direct window (direct = true)
nodes.rationale: Requested explicitly and justified: for a surface that changes wholesale, and for typography, since the compositor rasterises in the four faces the desktop chose. The trade is absolute - a direct window has no widgets, so its chrome is rectangles the application knows the position of. It buys the page and charges for the toolbar.

nodes.label: Window decoration and the full-width frame
nodes.rationale: BeOS made a tab only as wide as its title so stacked windows kept their titles readable; Kosmos does not stack windows, so it bought nothing, and the bar now spans the window with the border taking its colour.

nodes.label: Workspaces
nodes.rationale: BeOS had 32 with independent resolution each; here they are one more field in the window struct and a filter in the compositor.

nodes.label: Stack and tile
nodes.rationale: Haiku's two additions worth having from the start: several windows sharing one frame with tabs side by side, and attached windows that resize together. They come almost free out of the tab model.

nodes.label: Control-W, the one reserved key
nodes.rationale: The first version took Tab and the arrows, which decides no application may have a second control. With no modifiers to escape into, it takes screen and tmux's approach: one key that introduces a command rather than being one.

nodes.label: A press grabs
nodes.rationale: Everything until the release goes to the window and view the press landed in, even after the pointer has left; without it, releasing outside leaves two controls half-operated. A press on a title bar is the manager's, anywhere else is the application's.

nodes.label: Hover is not sent
nodes.rationale: Every movement would be a message and the path would run at the rate the pointer moves rather than at the rate anything changes. Movement is sent while a button is held, because that is what a control needs to un-press when you slide off it.

nodes.label: Compositing: damage, a cached backbuffer, one blit at vblank
nodes.rationale: If an app did not respond in time, compose with its previous command list and move on. Never block.

nodes.label: The cursor is part of the composite
nodes.rationale: Drawing it after the blit is cheaper and wrong: every repaint blits over it, and the display is scanned out on its own schedule, so it can be sampled in between - which looks like the cursor blinking on every click. It costs two rectangles of damage instead of one.

nodes.label: A window's damage waits until its drawing is finished
nodes.rationale: Commands arrive in several messages, so damaging after each one composites the window half-drawn. The surface is written either way; only the damage waits. That is what a backbuffer is for, applied one level up.

nodes.label: Replicants
nodes.rationale: A view is Lua source plus a state table, both serialisable, and a replicant is a message carrying source, state and needs; the host loads it and mounts exactly what needs declares. The honest limit: it runs inside its host's process, so the restriction is the language's rather than the kernel's - more than BeOS offered, less than a separate process. Evidence has to come from inside the replicant, not from the host.

nodes.label: The dimensional look
nodes.rationale: Reversed September 2026: committing to dimensionality is a design language, not a costume - raised means press this, sunken means content lives here, a groove means these are separate. Every desktop converges on the same flat rectangle, and Kosmos owes compatibility to nothing. The surviving rule: copy behaviour that was got right, decide shading fresh.

nodes.label: Themes, and colours named rather than captured
nodes.rationale: The palette table is mutated in place, never replaced, so every widget reading theme.text at draw time follows the change with nothing subscribing. A colour may be a number or a palette name resolved on every draw; capturing theme.text_dim at construction freezes it, which left a light theme with near-invisible headings.

nodes.label: What is not copied from BeOS
nodes.rationale: The C++ class hierarchy, BLooper as a system thread, the entire locking API, the four-byte what codes, and the Translation Kit. The hierarchy existed because 1990s C++ had no better way to express composition.

nodes.label: The UI build order
nodes.rationale: Windows, view tree, follow modes, basic widgets done at M6; workspaces, stack and tile, replicants and shared-memory surfaces at M7.
